blocks.text: Design a continuous integration and continuous delivery pipeline system, the mechanism that takes a single commit or merge and runs a defined set of stages, build, test, lint, deploy, against it, automatically. This is the third problem in this project's Asynchronous Systems category, and its defining shape is a dependency graph within one single run: some stages must wait for others to genuinely succeed first, while stages with no dependency relationship between them should run fully in parallel, and a failure anywhere should stop only the work that actually depended on it, never everything else.
blocks.content: Design a continuous integration and continuous delivery pipeline system, the mechanism that takes a single commit or merge and runs a defined set of stages, build, test, lint, deploy, against it, automatically. This is the third problem in this project's Asynchronous Systems category, and its defining shape is a dependency graph within one single run: some stages must wait for others to genuinely succeed first, while stages with no dependency relationship between them should run fully in parallel, and a failure anywhere should stop only the work that actually depended on it, never everything else.

blocks.alt: A commit triggers a pipeline whose stages form a dependency graph: a stage runs once its dependencies succeed, independent stages run concurrently, and a stage failure skips only the stages that depend on it

blocks.text: The two techniques that define this design are dependency-graph-based stage scheduling, where a stage becomes eligible to run only once every one of its declared dependencies has genuinely succeeded, with independent stages sharing no dependency relationship running fully in parallel rather than being needlessly serialized, and fail-fast propagation, where a stage's failure automatically skips every stage that depends on it, directly or transitively, while leaving every unrelated, independent stage to continue completely unaffected.

blocks.text: A user should be able to define a pipeline as a set of stages, each with zero or more declared dependencies on other stages. A commit or merge should trigger a run of that pipeline. A stage should only begin executing once every one of its declared dependencies has succeeded. Stages with no dependency relationship between them should execute concurrently rather than waiting on each other. If a stage fails, every stage that depends on it, directly or transitively, should be marked skipped rather than executed, while every stage with no dependency on the failed one should continue and complete entirely normally.

blocks.text: Five qualities matter here, and the second and third are in a natural, deliberate tension the fail-fast mechanism exists to resolve correctly.

blocks.alt: A stage never starts before its dependencies genuinely succeed, independent stages run in parallel, a failure stops only what actually depended on it, feedback arrives as fast as the graph allows, and the same commit produces the same result every time

blocks.text: A stage never starting before its dependencies genuinely succeed matters because deploying before tests have actually passed would defeat the entire purpose of having a pipeline at all. Independent stages running in parallel means two unrelated stages, like linting and unit testing, should never wait on each other for no structural reason. A failure stopping only dependent work means a failing lint stage should never stop a completely unrelated, independent test stage from finishing its own run. Fast feedback means a developer waiting on a pipeline result expects it as quickly as the dependency graph's own structure genuinely allows, not artificially slower. And reproducibility means the exact same commit run twice should not sometimes pass and sometimes fail for unrelated, non-deterministic reasons.

blocks.text: This design assumes that when a stage fails, only its actual dependents are skipped, while every independent, unrelated stage that is already running or not yet started is allowed to continue and complete entirely normally, since cancelling unrelated work provides no benefit and only destroys otherwise-useful feedback. Cycle validation in the dependency graph is assumed to happen at pipeline definition time, before any run is ever triggered, keeping the run-time scheduling logic itself simple, since a validated graph is guaranteed to be a genuine DAG. Secrets scoping is assumed to withhold sensitive credentials entirely from any stage triggered by an untrusted context, such as an external pull request, rather than attempting to selectively redact what a stage can do with them.

blocks.text: A large engineering organization can realistically trigger thousands of pipeline runs across a single busy day, with a single pipeline run capable of fanning out into dozens of independent, parallel-eligible stages at once. Fast feedback matters throughout, since a developer is often actively waiting on the result before continuing their own work.

blocks.text: A commit or merge trigger reaches the pipeline orchestrator, which hands the pipeline's defined stages to the dependency graph resolver. The resolver continuously identifies which stages have become eligible, every declared dependency already succeeded, and hands each eligible stage to the build runner pool, which reads from and writes to the build artifact and cache store as it executes.

blocks.alt: A trigger reaches the pipeline orchestrator, which resolves the stage dependency graph and hands eligible stages to a build runner pool backed by an artifact and cache store

blocks.text: Each stage carries its own declared list of dependencies. A stage becomes eligible to actually start executing only once every one of those dependencies has genuinely succeeded, or immediately if it has no dependencies at all. Until then, it simply stays waiting, not yet eligible.

blocks.alt: A stage becomes eligible to run only once every one of its declared dependencies has succeeded, or immediately if it has none at all

blocks.text: Once a stage's dependencies are satisfied, every other stage sharing that same satisfied dependency but with no dependency on each other runs fully concurrently. Two such independent branches, running unit tests and running lint checks are the classic example, never wait on one another, since neither one's own definition depends on the other at all.

blocks.text: When a stage fails during execution, every stage that depends on it, directly or transitively through the graph, is marked skipped and never actually attempted. Any stage with no dependency relationship to the failed one is entirely unaffected, continuing to run or completing normally exactly as if the failure had never happened.

blocks.text: A stage's dependency list is modeled as part of the pipeline's own definition, read once per run to build that run's dependency graph, while each individual stage execution's live status is modeled as fast-changing, per-run state, updated frequently as stages become eligible, start, and finish. Build artifacts are modeled separately, keyed by a content-derived identity so an unchanged dependency genuinely produces a cache hit rather than depending on run-specific metadata.

blocks.alt: Build succeeding makes both test and lint eligible at once, and the two run fully concurrently since neither depends on the other
Test failing leaves lint, an independent stage, unaffected and successful, while deploy, which depends on both, is correctly skipped rather than run

blocks.text: The happy path is the parallel execution flow above, independent stages running concurrently once their shared dependency succeeds. The workflow worth walking through separately is a partial failure: rather than either cancelling the entire run indiscriminately, which would throw away a lint stage's otherwise-useful, already-completed result, or silently ignoring the failure and running deploy anyway, which would defeat the pipeline's entire purpose, fail-fast propagation walks the dependency graph precisely, skipping exactly the stages that genuinely depended on the failure and nothing more.

blocks.alt: A stage whose dependencies are unchanged since the last run reuses an already-cached, equivalent build artifact instead of rebuilding it from scratch

blocks.text: Caching build artifacts keyed by their actual content, rather than by run number or timestamp, is what makes an unchanged dependency genuinely reusable across otherwise unrelated pipeline runs, meaningfully reducing both total build time and compute cost.

blocks.alt: Every stage that becomes eligible across every in-progress run is placed into a shared build runner queue, drained by a pool of runners executing many stages concurrently

blocks.text: Feeding every eligible stage, across every currently running pipeline, into one shared runner queue is what allows genuinely independent stages, even from entirely different pipeline runs, to execute concurrently against a shared pool of compute rather than each run needing its own dedicated capacity.
blocks.content: Feeding every eligible stage, across every currently running pipeline, into one shared runner queue is what allows genuinely independent stages, even from entirely different pipeline runs, to execute concurrently against a shared pool of compute rather than each run needing its own dedicated capacity.

blocks.alt: An eligible stage ready to execute is assigned to whichever runner in the shared pool is currently free

blocks.text: Because eligibility is already fully resolved by the dependency graph before a stage ever reaches the runner pool, load balancing itself can be a simple, ordinary least-busy-runner assignment, with no need to reason about dependency ordering at this layer at all.

blocks.alt: Runner queue depth across all in-progress pipeline runs growing faster than the runner pool can drain triggers adding more runners to the shared pool

blocks.text: Scaling here means growing the shared runner pool in response to overall eligible-stage volume across every active pipeline run, entirely independent of how many distinct pipelines or dependency graphs happen to be defined.

blocks.text: Pipeline definitions scale as a small, infrequently-changing, easily cached dataset. Stage execution state scales per active run and is naturally short-lived, cleaned up or archived once a run completes. Build artifacts scale as a large, content-addressed store, similar in spirit to this project's existing content-addressable chunk deduplication design, since the same underlying goal, avoiding redundant storage of identical content, applies here too.

blocks.alt: A stage's own current status within one specific run is strongly consistent, it cannot be both skipped and successful at once; whether a cached build artifact is still considered valid is only eventually consistent

blocks.text: A single stage's own status within its own run must be unambiguous at all times, since the fail-fast propagation logic depends directly on reading it correctly, while a slightly stale cache validity check has no correctness consequence, it only ever costs an unnecessary rebuild, never an incorrect result.

blocks.alt: A single build runner failing or disconnecting mid-execution has that stage reassigned to a different, healthy runner, continuing the pipeline run without restarting it entirely from the beginning

blocks.text: Because the runner pool is a stateless execution layer sitting below the dependency graph resolver, an individual runner failing is a routine, easily recovered event, only the one affected stage needs to be reassigned and re-attempted, the run's own overall progress and every other stage's status is completely unaffected.

blocks.alt: A stage running in a trusted, verified context has secrets injected only for its own execution; a stage triggered from an untrusted context, such as an external pull request, has secrets withheld entirely

blocks.text: Safe handling of deployment credentials and similar secrets is this design's defining security concern, distinct from every other category's angle in this project, since a pipeline by its nature often needs genuinely powerful credentials, and an untrusted external contributor's pull request triggering a run must never be able to exfiltrate them.

blocks.text: Per-stage execution duration is the most important thing to watch, a stage that many others transitively depend on becoming unusually slow directly delays every one of its dependents, and by extension the whole run's feedback time. The rate of stages skipped due to fail-fast propagation is also worth tracking over time, a rising trend can signal a genuinely flaky, frequently-failing upstream stage worth investigating directly.

blocks.text: Content-addressed build artifact caching is the largest cost optimization here, avoiding redundant, expensive rebuild work for dependencies that genuinely have not changed between runs. Running the shared runner pool across every active pipeline run, rather than provisioning dedicated capacity per pipeline, also keeps overall compute cost proportional to genuine total demand rather than the number of distinct pipelines defined.

blocks.text: A change to the dependency graph resolver's own eligibility logic needs the most rigorous possible testing in this system, since any bug there risks either a stage starting before its dependencies genuinely succeeded, a serious correctness failure, or a stage being incorrectly skipped despite its dependencies having actually succeeded, a serious availability failure. Dependency graphs themselves deserve periodic review for unnecessary edges, since an overly conservative graph silently costs real parallelism without providing any genuine correctness benefit.

blocks.text: Retrying a single failed stage in place, re-evaluating only its own dependents' eligibility rather than requiring an entire fresh run, could be layered on top of this same dependency graph architecture without changing its core scheduling guarantees. Dynamic, historical-duration-aware runner allocation, prioritizing runners for stages that many others transitively depend on, would further reduce total feedback time for the most structurally important stages in a given graph.

items: Architecture: dependency-graph-based stage scheduling that runs independent stages in parallel, paired with fail-fast propagation that skips only a failed stage's genuine dependents.
Capacity: thousands of pipeline runs a day for a large organization, with a single run capable of fanning out into dozens of parallel-eligible stages.
The core techniques: DAG-based eligibility scheduling and fail-fast dependent-skipping, both worked through with a real, verified implementation in Java, Python, and C++.
Database: pipeline definitions as small, cacheable configuration, per-run stage execution state, and a content-addressed build artifact and cache store.
End-to-end workflows: a normal parallel execution flow and a fail-fast flow, both traced as sequence diagrams.
Consistency: a strongly consistent per-run stage status, paired with an eventually consistent build artifact cache validity check.

Trade-offs: dependency-graph scheduling with fail-fast propagation versus strictly sequential execution versus cancelling an entire run on any failure, compared directly on parallelism and failure blast radius.
